statements.claim: Krishna and Balarama returned to Dwaraka carrying six small children, and word ran ahead that they had brought children back from the underworld.
statements.evidence: SB 10.85.51-56 pack excerpt: 'Taking the six sons, Krishna and Balarama return to Dwaraka and give them to their mother'; corpus chain DKS_0293 (Sutala visit) supplies the underworld origin.

statements.claim: The children were Devaki's sons; years before, her brother Kamsa had taken each of her first six children at birth and killed them, because a prophecy warned that a child of Devaki would end his reign.
statements.evidence: Corpus chain: DKS_0292/0293 context (evt_0498) — Devaki's 'sons slain by the Bhoja king', six sons born in her womb and slain by Kamsa (SB 10.85.47-49); the prophecy is established in the earlier Kamsa arc (corpus DKS_0003-0011).

statements.claim: She had raised Krishna and Balarama, the seventh and the eighth, and had loved them with all her strength.
statements.evidence: No support in this pack (SB 10.85.51-56), and it runs against the corpus's own canon: Krishna was handed to Vasudeva on the night of his birth and raised by Nanda and Yashoda in Vraja, and Balarama was transferred to Rohini's womb and raised in Vraja — Devaki was imprisoned until Krishna returned to Mathura as a boy of ~11 (corpus Vraja arc, e.g. DKS_0016 eleven years in Vraja). Devaki is the birth-mother of the seventh and eighth children; nothing in the corpus has her raising them from infancy.

statements.claim: Krishna and Balarama had descended to Sutala, the netherworld kingdom where King Bali reigned, and brought the six back to the world above.
statements.evidence: Corpus chain DKS_0293 (SB 10.85.34-49): 'Entering Sutala by their yoga-maya, Krishna and Balarama are received by the daitya king Bali'; the six released sons dwelt there awaiting release.

statements.claim: Devaki came out as they reached the gate, counted the six, her milk came, and she took them into her arms, nursing and embracing them, weeping and laughing.
statements.evidence: SB 10.85.52-53: 'devakī putra-sneha-snuta-stanī... apāyayat stanaṃ prītā suta-sparśa-parisnutam'; pack excerpt: 'Devaki, her breasts flowing with milk, nurses and embraces them.'

statements.claim: When the six had drunk their fill they bowed — first to Krishna, then Devaki, then Vasudeva, then Balarama — and, released from the curse, rose and ascended before the eyes of all to the abode of the gods.
statements.evidence: SB 10.85.54-56: 'te namaskṛtya govindaṃ devakīṃ pitaraṃ balam... mṛtāgamana-nirgamam'; pack excerpt: 'released from the curse, they bow and ascend to the gods' abode.' Bow order matches the verse (Govinda, Devaki, father/Vasudeva, Bala).

statements.claim: Devaki stood with empty arms and milk on her lips, the old grief gone out of her; the court and Dwaraka long remembered the night a curse was dissolved in a mother's embrace.
statements.evidence: Reflective close consistent with the pack (reunion, nursing, ascent); the 'single evening' duration and the city's lasting memory are narrative atmosphere not asserted by the pack but contradicted by nothing.

corrections.original_sentence: She had raised Krishna and Balarama, the seventh and the eighth, and had loved them with all her strength; but the six were always there, six small absences standing in the shadow of her heart.
corrections.suggested: She had borne Krishna and Balarama, the seventh and the eighth, and had loved them with all her strength; but the six were always there, six small absences standing in the shadow of her heart.

notes: Reunion, nursing, bowing and ascent all map cleanly to SB 10.85.51-56. One UNSUPPORTED biographical claim: 'she had raised Krishna and Balarama' — the corpus has both boys raised in Vraja (Krishna by Nanda/Yashoda after the birth-night handover; Balarama by Rohini after the womb-transfer), with Devaki imprisoned until Krishna's return to Mathura at ~11. Devaki is their birth-mother, so 'borne' preserves the sentence's intent.

statements.claim: Two men in Mithila — the brahmana Shrutadeva and King Bahulashva — each prepared to receive Krishna, each taking it for granted the visit was meant for him alone.
statements.evidence: SB 10.86.23-24: 'svānugrahāya samprāptaṃ manvānau taṃ jagad-gurum / nyamantrayetāṃ dāśārham ātithyena saha dvijaiḥ' (each thinking the world-guru had come for his own grace, they invited him with the brahmanas); pack excerpt names both hosts.

statements.claim: Krishna was traveling through the land with a company of sages; Shrutadeva was a brahmana of study and worship, Bahulashva the king of Mithila.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt: 'Krishna travels to Mithila with the sages... the brahmana Shrutadeva and King Bahulashva of Mithila'; verse 24 'saha dvijaiḥ'. Mithila's 'wise kings / no guest turned away' lore is generic atmosphere.

statements.claim: Each prepared with all his household — the brahmana swept his courtyard and set out food; the king hung garlands and called for musicians — and each invited Krishna and the sages to stay.
statements.evidence: The double invitation is supported (10.86.24); the specific preparations (swept courtyard, musicians) are invented domestic color, contradicting nothing in the pack.

statements.claim: The king, seeing the weary travelers approach, went out to meet them, his heart overflowing, eyes blurred with tears; with his whole family he bowed low and worshipped Krishna and the sages.
statements.evidence: SB 10.86.26-28: 'śrāntān apy atha tān dūrāj janakaḥ sva-gṛhāgatān / pravṛddha-bhaktyā uddharṣa-hṛdayāsrāvilekṣaṇaḥ / sa-kuṭumbo vahan mūrdhnā pūjayāṃ cakra īśvarān' (weary from afar, great devotion, heart thrilled, tear-filled eyes, bowing with his family).

statements.claim: The king said: 'Your own promise is being kept — let our eyes rest on you. Who would ever turn away from your lotus feet? You who came down into the line of Yadu for the sake of mortals wandering through the world — stay in our house for a few days, you and the brahmanas with you.'
statements.evidence: SB 10.86.31-35 (Bahulashva's speech): 'sva-vacas tad ṛtaṃ kartum asmad-dṛg-gocaro bhavān... ko nu tvac-caraṇāmbhojam... yo 'vatīrya yador vaṃśe nṛṇāṃ saṃsaratām iha... dināni katicid bhūman gṛhān no nivasa dvijaiḥ'.

statements.claim: In the same hour Krishna was seated in Shrutadeva's simple house, accepting whatever the brahmana offered with overflowing joy; Krishna was whole in both houses at once, fully present in each, and neither host saw the other or knew.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt: 'To please both devotees, Krishna enters both homes at once, unseen by either, and each worships him with overflowing devotion.'

statements.claim: Night fell; beneath each of the two lamps sat the same Lord; neither man ever learned the truth, and both families rose blessed, each believing its visit had been the only one.
statements.evidence: Consistent with the pack's 'unseen by either' during the double visit; the hosts' permanent mutual ignorance is a closing flourish — the pack's excerpt range (10.86.23-36) does not cover the aftermath, so nothing contradicts it.

notes: Faithful to SB 10.86.23-36 — the double invitation, Bahulashva's tearful welcome and speech (nearly line-by-line), and the simultaneous unseen presence in both houses all check out. Only connective domestic color and a closing flourish; no unsupported or contradicted facts.

statements.claim: In Dwaraka, a brahmana's newborn sons died one after another, dying as they met the ground.
statements.evidence: SB 10.89.21-24 and pack excerpt: 'A brahmana's infant sons die as soon as they touch the ground' — 'evaṃ dvitīyaṃ viprarṣis tṛtīyaṃ tv evam eva ca' (so the second, and the third in the same way).

statements.claim: The brahmana wrapped each dead child and laid it at the gate of the palace, and cried that the king's fault had slain his children.
statements.evidence: SB 10.89.21: 'vipro gṛhītvā mṛtakaṃ rāja-dvāry upadhāya saḥ'; pack excerpt: 'each time he lays the dead child at the palace gate, lamenting that the king's fault has slain his children.'

statements.claim: The brahmana accused the ruler as a man who hated brahmanas, crafty of mind, greedy, sunk in pleasure, delighting in violence, ill-behaved, master of nothing in himself, whose failure of duty makes his subjects perish in misery.
statements.evidence: SB 10.89.22-23: 'brahma-dviṣaḥ śaṭha-dhiyo lubdhasya viṣayātmanaḥ / hiṃsā-vihāraṃ nṛpatiṃ duḥśīlam ajitendriyam'; pack excerpt: 'accuses the unrighteous ruler of failing in his duty, so that his subjects perish in misery.'

statements.claim: The narrative staggers the outcry: the first son was buried quietly at home, the second laid at the gate in silence, and only at the third did the brahmana cry the accusation aloud before the city.
statements.evidence: Dramatic pacing for a sensitive scene (see content_note). The pack passage suggests the gate-complaint pattern applied from the first death (10.89.21-23 describing the lament, then v.24 'the second and the third in the same way'), so the story's quiet first burial is a softening deviation, not a denial of the canonical accusation.

statements.claim: The palace gates stayed shut, no one came out to answer the charge, and the watching crowd grew as the brahmana left the child where the guards could see it.
statements.evidence: Scene-setting consistent with the pack; the city's unresponsiveness and crowd are connective staging not stated in the excerpt.

statements.claim: Arjuna was in Dwaraka then, staying near Krishna; he heard the lament and asked the brahmana whether there was no bearer of the bow in the place where brahmanas weep, bereft of wealth, wives and children.
statements.evidence: SB 10.89.25-27: 'tām arjuna upaśrutya karhicit keśavāntike / kiṃ svid brahmaṃs tvan-nivāse iha nāsti dhanur-dharaḥ / dhana-dārātmajāpṛktā yatra śocanti brāhmaṇāḥ'.

statements.claim: The brahmana looked at Arjuna and said nothing; the answer would come with the next child.
statements.evidence: Bridge to the following episode (evt_0281); not asserted by the pack but contradicts nothing.

notes: Deaths, gate-laying, and the full catalogue of accusations map directly to SB 10.89.20-27, and Arjuna's intervention matches v.25-27. One staging note: the pack says the gate-lament pattern held 'each time' (v.24 'second and third in the same way'), while the story delays the public outcry to the third death for dramatic restraint; judged connective, flagged here for review.

statements.claim: Arjuna vowed to the brahmana that he would protect the next child, and that if even one more child was taken he would enter the fire.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt (SB 10.89.28-31): 'Arjuna... vows that he will protect the next child or enter fire'; v.28 'ahaṃ... rakṣiṣye dīnayor iha'.

statements.claim: The brahmana asked how Arjuna could do what is difficult even for the lords of the world.
statements.evidence: SB 10.89.30: 'tat kathaṃ nu bhavān karma duṣkaraṃ jagad-īśvaraiḥ'.

statements.claim: Arjuna answered, 'Do not look down on my strength — it is the strength that pleased Tryambaka himself,' and the brahmana was reassured.
statements.evidence: SB 10.89.32-33: 'māvamaṃsthā mama brahman vīryaṃ tryambaka-toṣaṇam / evaṃ viśrambhito vipraḥ' (the brahmana was thus made confident).

statements.claim: At the time of the birth Arjuna went to the brahmana's house, touched pure water, bowed to Maheshvara, and ringed the delivery room with a cage of arrows, shaft joined to shaft with every weapon in his art.
statements.evidence: SB 10.89.34-36: 'prasūti-kāla āsanne... sa upaspṛśya śucy ambho namaskṛtya maheśvaram / nyaruṇat sūtikāgāraṃ śarair nānāstra-yojitaiḥ'. The 'neither wind nor bird nor hand could pass' density is hyperbolic color on the supported cage.

statements.claim: The child was born and cried, and then, before Arjuna's eyes, was lifted bodily into the sky through the cage of arrows and vanished.
statements.evidence: SB 10.89.37: 'tataḥ kumāraḥ sañjāto vipra-patnyā rudan muhuḥ'; pack excerpt: 'the newborn vanishes bodily into the sky'. The 'through the arrows as if they were water' matches the HV telling of the same episode (Harivamsha 1.260, used in the DKS_0299 pack).

statements.claim: The brahmana, in the presence of Krishna, rebuked Arjuna: 'Neither Pradyumna, nor Aniruddha, nor Balarama, nor Keshava himself could save that child. Fie on Arjuna, the false speaker. Fie on the bow of the self-praiser.'
statements.evidence: SB 10.89.38-40: 'tadāha vipro vijayaṃ vinindan kṛṣṇa-sannidhau / na pradyumno nāniruddho na rāmo na ca keśavaḥ / dhig arjunaṃ mṛṣā-vādaṃ dhig ātma-ślāghino dhanuḥ' — names and curse match exactly.

statements.claim: His great bow, the bow that had pleased Shiva himself, hung at his side like a thing he no longer recognized.
statements.evidence: The pack's verse credits his valor/strength with pleasing Tryambaka (v.32 'vīryaṃ tryambaka-toṣaṇam'), not the bow itself; the phrase is loose synecdoche for the archer whose prowess pleased Shiva. Atmosphere after the public failure; not a storyline fact.

notes: Vow, cage of arrows, vanishing newborn, and the brahmana's curse all match SB 10.89.28-40 nearly line by line (including the exact order of names in the rebuke). The 'bow that pleased Shiva' is a synecdoche slip flagged in statements; no hard issues.

statements.claim: A brahmana had lost his four sons — three boys taken from him earlier, and then a newborn infant — and Krishna had promised to bring them back.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.260 (in pack): Krishna returned 'with the four sons of the Brāhmana and gave those three boys who had been stolen before and the new born baby into the hands of the Brāhmana'; promise and mission carried by corpus chain (DKS_0298, evt_0221).

statements.claim: The sea opened before their car: the lord of the ocean rose with folded hands, asked what he should do, pleaded that an opened way would tempt other kings to cross, and Krishna promised no one else would ever assail it; the waters held still and the car passed through the red depths as over land.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.260 (Dutt): ocean 'with folded hands' asks 'What am I to do?'; 'other kings, elated with the pride of their strength, will cross me by this way'; Krishna replies 'Save me no one else will be able to assail you'; 'we proceeded through that lustrous red water as if we were on land'.

statements.claim: Seven mountains bowed their crests and gave them passage, and they crossed the seven continents and seas and the ring of mountains that fences the world (Lokaloka).
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.260: seven mountains (Jayanta, Vaijayanta, Neela, Rajata, Mahāmeru, Kailasha, Indrakuta) 'saluting Govinda... gave him the passage'; 'crossing the seven insular continents, oceans and seven rivers as well as Lokaloka'. The story's 'seven seas' condenses the text's 'oceans'.

statements.claim: The horses faltered in a darkness thick as mud, and Krishna dispelled the darkness with his discus, parting it so the sky came back.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.260: 'I found the horses carrying the car with great difficulty... the darkness was owing to thick mud... Govinda dispelled that darkness and mud with his discus and the sky and the passage of the car became visible'.

statements.claim: Arjuna saw a bundle of effulgence in the form of a man spread across the heavens above all the worlds; Krishna walked into it while the brahmana and Arjuna waited, and within a moment returned with the four sons, whole and unharmed.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.260: 'I saw in the sky a bundle of effulgence, of the shape of a man, extending over all the worlds. Then Rishikesha entered into that bundle of effulgence and that best of Brāhmanas and myself waited on the car. Within a moment the powerful Krishna returned with the four sons.'

statements.claim: It was the Supreme Lord himself who had taken the children; he told them he had brought the brahmana's sons there because he wished to see Krishna and Arjuna, and that since the earth had been relieved of its burden the time had come for them to turn back.
statements.evidence: SB 10.89.57-58: 'dvijātmajā me yuvayor didṛkṣuṇā mayopanītā bhuvi dharma-guptaye / pūrṇa-kāmāv api yuvāṃ nara-nārāyaṇāv ṛṣī'; pack excerpt: 'he, wishing to see them, had himself brought the brahmana's sons to his abode, and that having slain the earth's burden they should now return.'

statements.claim: They returned by the way they came, the wonders repeating in reverse, and the car stood in Dwaraka with the first part of the day still unfinished.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.260: 'we... came out in the same way as we had gone there... arriving at Dwārakā within a moment we saw that even the first part of the day was not complete'; SB 10.89.59-60 'nyavartetāṃ svakaṃ dhāma... yathā-gatam'.

statements.claim: Krishna placed the four sons in their father's hands; the brahmana wept with joy, and Krishna fed him and his sons, gave him riches, and sent him away satisfied.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.260: 'Krishna returned with the four sons... gave... into the hands of the Brāhmana. Regaining his sons the Brāhmana was highly pleased... Krishna fed that Brāhmana with his sons and satisfying him with riches sent him away to his own house.'

statements.claim: Arjuna, having seen Vishnu's abode, felt every human power fall away — not his own doing but a gift flowing from Krishna's grace.
statements.evidence: SB 10.89.61: 'niśāmya vaiṣṇavaṃ dhāma pārthaḥ parama-vismitaḥ'; pack excerpt: 'Arjuna, astounded at the vision of Vishnu's abode, regards all human power as Krishna's grace.'

notes: Journey and restoration track Harivamsha 1.260 (Dutt, quoted in full in the pack) nearly incident by incident — ocean crossing, seven mountains, Lokaloka, discus-dispelled darkness, bundle of effulgence, return within the first part of the day, feeding and enrichment of the brahmana; the Lord's explanation matches SB 10.89.57-61. No unsupported or contradicted facts.

statements.claim: Men wondered afterward why Krishna, who could ride Garuda, kept the great bird walking at his side instead of mounting him on the road from Vidarbha.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.112 opening: Janamejaya asks why Krishna, setting out from the city of Bidarbha, 'did not ride the highly powerful son of Vinatā, Garuda; why did he then take him away with him?'

statements.claim: Before the assembled kings Krishna announced he would go to Mathura; Garuda saluted him and asked leave to fly first to Kushasthali, the old city of king Raivata at the foot of Mount Raivata on the bank of the great ocean.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.112 (4-7): Krishna 'said before the assembled kings, "I shall repair to the charming city of Mathura"'; Garuda: 'I shall now proceed to Raivata's city Kushasthali... It is situate at the base of the Raivata mountain and on the bank of the great ocean.'

statements.claim: Garuda described Kushasthali as abandoned by the rakshasas, with trees hung with filaments of flowers, groves and creepers like Nandana, and elephants, serpents, bears, monkeys, boars, buffaloes and deer moving through it; if worthy of Krishna's dwelling he would root out every thorn and come back.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.112 (8-10): 'The Rākshasas have abandoned the charming city of Kushasthali... abounds in trees decorated with filaments of flowers, in groves and creepers... scattered with elephants and serpents, and inhabited by bear, monkeys, boars, buffaloes and deer... if that extensive and charming city is fitted for thy residence, I shall remove all the thorns and come back to thee.'

statements.claim: Mathura had been won back from Kamsa, but Jarasandha — whose daughters had been married to the slain king — had already hurled his armies at the city and would hurl more, and Jarasandha could not be slain by them; Krishna said: 'O son of Vinata, the king Jarasandha is unslayable by us. It never bodes good for us to live in this city of Mathura.'
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.112 excerpt (verbatim): 'O Vinatā's son, the king Jarāsandha is unslayable by us... it never bodes good for us to live in this city of Mathura.' Jarasandha's daughters married to Kamsa and his earlier attacks are established in the corpus's Mathura arc (corpus chain DKS_0300 → evt_0190).

statements.claim: While Garuda was gone Krishna entered Mathura with the Yadavas, and Ugrasena — the old king restored to his throne — came out with dancing girls and citizens and honored the victorious Krishna; the city dressed itself in flags and garlands.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.112 (12, 14-22): 'when Krishna too, with the Yadavas, entered into the beautiful city of Mathurā, Ugrasena came out of the city with dancing girls and citizens and honored the victorious Krishna'; 'the city was decorated with flags, garlands of wild flowers and jars full of water.' Ugrasena's restoration is corpus Mathura-arc canon.

statements.claim: Garuda returned with a glad report: he had flown over Kushasthali wall by wall and found it worthy — at the foot of Raivata, emptied of its rakshasas, washed by the sea breeze — and brought the promise: 'Your city will be celebrated in the three worlds under the name of Dwaravati.'
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt: 'Garuda said: ... "thy city will be celebrated in the three worlds under the name of Dwāravati"'; index summary: 'Garuda returns from reconnoitering Kushasthali and praises it as a fitting abode.'

statements.claim: Krishna weighed what he knew — Jarasandha unslayable, Mathura small and open to every enemy — and resolved that when the time came the Yadavas would leave Mathura and follow where Garuda had flown.
statements.evidence: Index summary: 'Krishna, knowing Jarasandha unslayable, resolves to leave Mathura'; the fuller departure deliberation belongs to the next episode (HV 1.113, DKS_0301).

notes: Faithful to Harivamsha 1.112 (Dutt): Janamejaya's framing question, Garuda's description of Kushasthali, Krishna's unslayable-Jarasandha speech (verbatim), Ugrasena's welcome, and the Dwaravati promise all check out. The 'flown wall by wall' reconnoiter sits in the portion of the chapter summarized by the pack's index entry; no contradictions.

statements.claim: No enemy threw the Yadavas out of Mathura; they left of their own counsel, on a day they chose themselves.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.113: the Yadavas, hearing of the approach of Jarasandha and Kalayavana, 'thought of retreating as mentioned before', and Krishna himself declares 'To day is an auspicious day. So we shall, even this very day, issue out of Mathura' — an unforced, self-chosen departure.

statements.claim: Jarasandha, emperor of Magadha, had come against Mathura and been beaten back, but he could not be slain — destined deathless to his enemies — and his soldiers were so many the Yadavas could not have destroyed them even in a hundred years of war.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.113 (10-11): 'Our enemy the king Jarāsandha has been destined as unslayable by us... so great is the number of his soldiers that we shall not be able to bring about their destruction even in hundred years'; earlier repelled sieges are corpus Mathura-arc canon.

statements.claim: Word came that Kalayavana, a foreign king of terrible strength, was marching on the city with an akshouhini of soldiers, and his messenger had already come to the houses of the Vrishnis and the Andhakas; the clans gathered, made Krishna their president, and held their conference in fear.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.113 excerpt: 'starting for Mathura with one Akshouhini of soldiers Kalayavana sent his messenger to the house of Vrishnis and Andhakas... making the highly intelligent Krishna their president, held a conference in fear of Kalayavana.'

statements.claim: Krishna told the Yadus in assembly: Mathura is the abode of the Yadavas; we were born here and grew up in Vraja; our griefs are gone and enemies defeated, but hostilities with the kings and the war with Jarasandha have begun; though our infantry, animals, jewels and friends are without number, Mathura is small and an enemy can enter it easily, and a crore of princes and soldiers crowded here would breed dissension; better to live elsewhere and lay out a new city, which he would carry out at the proper time if they approved.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.113 (1-8) — the assembly speech is reproduced nearly point by point, including 'one Koti of princes and infantry... dissension cropping up' and 'if you like it, we will lay out a city elsewhere'.

statements.claim: The Yadavas answered with one voice: 'Do what you deem proper for the good of all of us.'
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.113 (9): 'Hearing it all the Yādavas delightedly said:—"O Krishna, do what thou deemst proper for the behoof of all these people"'.

statements.claim: Then came the news that Jarasandha and Kalayavana were advancing together with an army too vast to count; the elders consulted and saw that a hundred years of war could not finish that host; Krishna declared the day auspicious and ordered the departure that very day with army and followers.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.113 (10-14): 'the emperor Jarāsandha, along with Kālayavana was proceeding towards Mathurā with his army... To day is an auspicious day. So we shall, even this very day, issue out of Mathura along with our army and followers.'

statements.claim: They went out that same day headed by Vasudeva — wives, children, chariots, elephants — the noise of the march like the waves of the ocean; they left with their wealth, kinsmen, friends, golden chariots, infuriated elephants and gold-harnessed horses, set their faces to the west, and Vasudeva and the other elders rode in front guiding the columns.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.113 (15-20): 'the Yadavas, headed by Vasudeva, along with their wives, cars and elephants, set out, echoing the four quarters with the noise of their soldiers resembling that of the waves of the ocean... set out for the west. Stationed in front, Vasudeva and other leading Yadavas... guided the army.'

statements.claim: They reached the bank of the sea — variegated with creepers, rich in coconut trees, covered with ketaki, palmyra and vines — and were as delighted as if they had arrived at the celestial region; Krishna found an extensive tract on the ocean's edge with coppery soil mixed with gravel, good for beasts of burden, marked with every favorable sign of a city as if presided over by the Goddess of Prosperity, fanned by the sea breeze and watered by the ocean.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.113 (21-29): 'It was variegated with creepers, abounded in coconut trees... covered with Ketaki trees, palmyras, Pannages and vines... the Yadavas were highly delighted as if they had arrived at the celestial region... The land had a coppery soil mixed with gravels, was well-suited for animals of burden, was endued with all the favourable marks of a city, as if it was presided over by the Goddess of prosperity herself. It was fanned by the sea breeze and was watered by the ocean.'

statements.claim: Near the site rose Mount Raivata, shining like Mandara, where Drona had lived for many years and King Ekalavya had once made his home, and the sporting ground that already bore the name Dwaravati; there Krishna chose his site and the Yadava commanders pitched tents for the night.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.113 (25-31): 'Near it was shining in beauty the charming mountain Raivata like the mount Mandara... Drona lived for many long years. There lived the king Ekalavya. And the sporting ground laid out by himself like a board of dice is celebrated by the name of Dwāravati... Keshava selected that site for his city... the Yadu commanders pitched tents there for the night.'

statements.claim: Standing on the new ground, the foremost of the Yadavas — Gada's younger brother, the leader of them all — thought of the names he would give to the houses of the city, and rested shorn of anxiety; the Yadavas secured Dwaravati and lived there happily with their friends, as the gods live in their own city.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.113 (32-35): 'the leader of the Yādavas, having Gada as his elder brother, thought in his mind of the names he would give to the various houses in that city... having thus secured the city of Dwaravati the Yādavas, along with their friends, lived there happily as do the gods in their own city.' (The 'Gada's younger brother' phrasing mirrors the Dutt translation, which here makes Gada the elder.)

notes: Nearly a paraphrase of Harivamsha 1.113 (Dutt): Krishna's assembly speech, the Yadavas' one-voice assent, the Jarasandha-Kalayavana advance, the same-day departure headed by Vasudeva, the coastal site with its coppery soil, Mount Raivata with Drona and Ekalavya, the pre-existing name Dwaravati, and the naming of future houses all match the passage in order. No unsupported or contradicted facts.

statements.claim: Rukmi of Vidarbha, who had spent his life showing rivalry toward Krishna, announced a swayamvara for his daughter, and rich and powerful kings and princes came to his house from many countries.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.118 (1-2, 12): 'the powerful Rukshmi... announced that his daughter would make her choice of a husband... many rich and powerful kings and princes came to his house from various countries'; 'the king Rukshmi used always to show rivalry with Krishna.'

statements.claim: With the other princes came Pradyumna, the son of Krishna and Rukmini; the moment she saw him, Rukmi's daughter Rukmavati wanted to marry him — she was celebrated on earth for her beauty, endowed with grace and radiance — and Krishna's son, peerless in beauty, wished to espouse her in turn.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.118 (3-4): 'Prādyumna, accompanied by other princes, went there. As soon as she saw him Rukshmini's daughter wanted to marry him. She too, endued with grace and effulgence, was celebrated on earth for her beauty. Keshava's son therefore wished to espouse that one of fair eyes.'

statements.claim: When the kings were seated in the swayamvara hall, the princess of Vidarbha chose Pradyumna, the slayer of enemies — a master of arms, well-built like a lion, the most handsome young man in the assembly.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.118 (5-6): 'when all the powerful kings took their seats in the Swayamvara hall, the Bidarbha king's daughter chose Pradyumna the slayer of enemies... For he was a master of arms and well-built like a lion. Besides Keshava's son was peerless in beauty on earth.'

statements.claim: After the ceremony the kings returned to their cities and Pradyumna went home to Dwaraka with the princess of Vidarbha; he lived happily with her, as Nala lived with Damayanti, and in time she bore him a son, Aniruddha, like the son of a god, of matchless deeds.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.118 (8-9): 'After the termination of the Swayamvara the kings repaired to their respective cities and Pradyumna too went to Dwārakā with the princess of Bidarbha with him. The hero lived happily in her company as did Nala in that of Damayanti. Pradyumna begat on her a son by name Aniruddha, like unto the son of a god and of matchless deeds on earth.'

statements.claim: Aniruddha came of age and mastered the Vedas, the science of archery, and the moral laws; then Krishna chose a wife for him — Rukmavati again, the granddaughter of Rukmi, gold-like in beauty, namesake of the elder Rukmavati who had married Pradyumna.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.118 (9-11): 'When, Aniruddha, coming of age, mastered the Vedas, the science of archery and the moral laws, Mādhava selected the beautiful gold-like Rukshmavati, the grand-daughter of Rukshmi, for his wife.' The namesake point follows from both brides bearing the same name in the source.

statements.claim: For the eagerness of his son and of Rukmini, Rukmi set aside his old enmity and said with delight: 'I confer Rukmavati on Aniruddha, endued with accomplishments and of a peaceful nature.'
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.118 (12-13): 'still, on account of the eagerness of his son and Rukshmini he cast off his enmity and said with delightedness "I confer Rukshmavati on Aniruddha endued with accomplishments and of a peaceful nature"'.

statements.claim: Krishna went to Vidarbha surrounded by his own army, accompanied by Rukmini, Balarama, his sons and the other Yadavas; Rukmi's kinsmen, friends and allies came at his invitation, and on an auspicious day under a favorable planet the wedding of Aniruddha and Rukmavati was celebrated with great festivity, the Vidarbhas and Yadavas rejoicing together and the Vrishnis honored there like immortals.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.118 (14-15, 19-20): 'Keshava, surrounded by his own army and accompanied by Rukshmini, Sangkarshana, his own sons and other Yādavas, went to Bidarbha... Rukshmi's kinsmen, friends and allies came there also at his invitation... in an auspicious day and under the auspicies of a favourable planet Aniruddha's wedding was celebrated with great festivity... the Baidharvas and the Yadavas performed a great festivity. And adored there like immortals the Vrishnis lived happily.'

statements.claim: For those days at least, the old quarrel between the two houses was remembered by no one.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.118 (12-13): Rukmi 'cast off his enmity' for the marriage, and both houses feasted together; the time-scoped phrasing ('for those days at least') stays within what the source shows.

statements.claim: The feud that had once divided Vidarbha from Dwaraka ended not in a treaty but in a wedding, and the two families sat down together as one.
statements.evidence: The pack's own continuation of Harivamsha 1.118 (verses 16-38, quoted in the passage) shows the enmity alive immediately after the wedding: Rukmi 'used always to show rivalry with Krishna' (v.12), and right after the festivities he conspires with the Deccan chiefs 'to vanquish Revati's husband' at dice and gloats over Baladeva's losses ('the highly wily Rukshmi... with pride... "Baladeva... has lost innumerable gold coins to me"'). The rivalry was set aside for the wedding, not ended by it.

corrections.original_sentence: The feud that had once divided Vidarbha from Dwaraka ended not in a treaty but in a wedding, and the two families sat down together as one.
corrections.suggested: The feud that had once divided Vidarbha from Dwaraka was set aside for those days, and the two families sat down together as one.

notes: Swayamvara, Pradyumna-Rukmavati marriage, Aniruddha's education, and the second Rukmavati wedding all track Harivamsha 1.118 nearly verbatim. One CONTRADICTED closing flourish: the story declares the feud between the houses 'ended' by the wedding, but the pack's own passage continues past the festivities into Rukmi's immediate conspiracy to cheat and humiliate Balarama at dice — his enmity was laid aside for the occasion, not ended. The immediately preceding sentence ('For those days at least...') is properly scoped and supported; only the final unqualified claim needs the correction.
